subject: History
title: Y7 History — Deep Time and Ancient World Unit Sequence
tool_context: Y7 History year sequence covering two content units (Deep Time: First Nations Australians; Ancient World: one ancient society) with the historical skills strand (S01–S08) woven in progressively. Skills are introduced at the point of first genuine application within each content descriptor phase.
progression_endpoint: Students produce historical descriptions, explanations, and arguments about First Nations Australians' deep-time history and an ancient society, drawing on historical knowledge, concepts, and terms and referencing evidence from primary and secondary sources — demonstrating that they can ask historical questions, locate and analyse sources, explain causes and continuity/change, identify perspectives and interpretations, and communicate historical reasoning.

phases.label: Inquiry Foundations
phases.checkpoint: Students can use BP, BCE, and CE dating conventions correctly, develop historical inquiry questions using at least two concept frames, and locate and classify primary and secondary sources using a digital repository.

waypoints.note: BP, BCE/CE conventions established before Deep Time content — chronological fluency is a prerequisite for all subsequent historical reasoning.

phases.label: Early Human Migration
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe competing theories of human evolution and migration, explain how environmental changes drove movement out of Africa, and identify how different evidence types inform historical interpretations.

waypoints.note: Origin and content analysis introduced using K01 evidence types — stratigraphy results, radiocarbon dating reports, oral history records.
Accuracy assessment first applied to K01 evidence — distinguishing fact from interpretation in claims about early human migration.

phases.label: Arrival on the Australian Continent
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe theories about the causes and effects of First Nations Australians' arrival on the continent, explain migration routes using geographical and chronological evidence, and sort and organise sources by type.

waypoints.note: Sorting and organising sources for the K02 inquiry — archaeological sites, DNA research, geographical evidence.
Multi-causal reasoning applied to the causes of migration and dispersal across the continent.

phases.label: Continuity over Deep Time
phases.checkpoint: Students can explain deep time as a historical concept, describe specific evidence for cultural continuity and change across deep time, and apply context and purpose analysis to deep-time sources.

waypoints.note: Context and purpose analysis applied to deep-time sources — rock art, oral tradition records, archaeological site reports.
Continuity/change framework applied to First Nations Australians' cultures across deep time.

phases.label: Environmental Response over Time
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe major environmental changes and their geographical consequences, explain how oral traditions preserve evidence of those changes, and identify perspectives embedded in deep-time sources.

waypoints.note: Perspective analysis introduced using deep-time sources — oral traditions, rock art, archaeological reports.

phases.label: Early Technological Achievements
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe stone tool technologies, food production systems, and land and water management technologies — explaining how each developed across different environments and contributed to daily life.

phases.label: Social Organisation and Cultural Practice
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe kinship, moiety, and totem systems, explain oral traditions as a cultural transmission mechanism, and identify attitudes and values of the past expressed in cultural sources.

waypoints.note: Attitudes and values of the past read through deep-time cultural sources — oral traditions, social organisation systems, cultural practices.

phases.label: Cultural Preservation and Heritage
phases.checkpoint: Students can explain cultural obligations around heritage sites and ancestral remains, describe the Lake Mungo case, explain the roles of multiple stakeholders in cultural preservation, and produce a historical description using historical terms and source references.

waypoints.note: Usefulness vs accuracy distinction applied to heritage sources — oral tradition and repatriation case evidence where accuracy is contested but usefulness is high.
First historical description output — describing a Deep Time topic using historical terms and source references.

phases.label: Historical and Archaeological Evidence
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe stratigraphy, DNA testing, written sources, and conservation as methods for investigating early societies, and apply full OCCP source analysis to ancient society sources.

waypoints.note: Full OCCP integration applied to ancient society sources — synthesising all four dimensions to assess what each source can and cannot reveal.

phases.label: Environment and Ancient Development
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe the physical geography of the ancient society's location and explain how it shaped agricultural development, social complexity, settlement patterns, and trade.

phases.label: Roles and Groups in Ancient Society
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe the roles and power mechanisms of key social groups, explain that evidence about underrepresented groups is limited but still revealing, and identify perspectives absent from the historical record.

waypoints.note: Absent perspectives applied to the ancient society — which groups are underrepresented, why, and what limited evidence reveals.
Integrated accuracy and usefulness assessment applied across the full set of ancient society source types.

phases.label: Beliefs, Values and Practices
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe the religious beliefs and practices of their chosen focus area, connect beliefs to practices using evidence, and explain what these reveal about the ancient society's values.

phases.label: Contacts, Conflicts and Change
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe the causes and effects of significant contacts and conflicts — including conquest, trade expansion, and peace treaties — and explain these as drivers of historical change.

phases.label: Significant Individual
phases.checkpoint: Students can describe the role and achievements of a significant individual, connect their significance to the broader historical context, explain why historians have interpreted them differently, and produce a historical explanation using historical concepts and source evidence.

waypoints.note: Historical interpretation introduced through the significant individual — why different historians have assessed their legacy differently.
Historical explanation as the Ancient unit output — explaining causation, significance, or continuity/change using historical concepts and source evidence.

phases.label: Historical Argument — Extended
phases.checkpoint: Students can develop and communicate a full historical argument drawing on knowledge and sources from both units — taking a position on significance, causation, or interpretation, supporting it with evidence, and acknowledging an alternative view. This is the mature form of the historical argument capability first developed in earlier phases.

waypoints.note: Historical argument about interpretation — integrating interpretation analysis from across both units into a full argument structure.
Extended historical argument as capstone — the full demand of S08, drawing on the complete K-strand knowledge base and all S-strand skills built across the year.
